<Rep. Frank Pallone, Jr.>: We oppose H.R. 161, the ``New Source Review Permitting Improvement Act,'' which amends the Clean Air Act (CAA) to allow increases in cancer causing pollution at facilities by manipulating how emissions are measured under the New Source Review (NSR) program, and creating sweeping exemptions for nearly every facility from having to install pollution controls.
BACKGROUND
The CAA requires the owner or operator of any new or expanded source of air pollution to obtain permits before construction begins, ensuring that new and expanding facilities will not increase pollution above levels that are safe to breathe. The preconstruction permitting provisions achieve this by requiring new and modified sources to use control technology to reduce their emissions; and to assess, and, if necessary, address their remaining air quality impacts. EPA's NSR program includes three different types of permitting requirements that depend on the size of a facility and the air quality where a facility will be located. The vast majority of the NSR permitting is done by the states, with the experts at EPA providing guidance and technical assistance.
For nonattainment areas, which already have dangerous, unhealthy air, the facility owner or operator must obtain a preconstruction permit under the nonattainment NSR program. This program is the subject of H.R. 161 and applies to both new major sources and existing sources that are undergoing major modifications. NSR permits require the installation of pollution controls that are sufficient to meet the lowest achievable emission rate, emission offsets from existing sources, and the opportunity for public involvement.
The proponents of this bill claim the definition of ``modification'' is too broad and would catch upgrades to facilities that might not impact emissions. They also stated concerns that this would reduce facility investment and stymie growth. However, the CAA has a history of spurring innovation and investments, especially in emissions reduction technologies.
SUMMARY OF H.R. 161
Section 2 amends Section 111 of the CAA to change the accounting for emissions from an annual rate to a new ``maximum hourly emission rate'' in a preceding 10-year period. This is a weaker test leading to pollution controls being required only if a polluter managed to exceed--implausibly--its vastly higher capacity to emit air pollution, measured from some point in the plant's past. Aging facilities could expand without permits, while increasing annual pollution so long as the hourly potential emissions did not change. A state regulatory witness confirmed this change would be an increased burden on states with air permitting primacy and recordkeeping.\1\ This change would also make the regulatory process more burdensome for industry and regulators (requiring 10 years of hourly emissions records), less transparent, and allow for miscalculations and interference to impact critical emissions data.
\1\House Committee on Energy and Commerce, Testimony of Ali Mirzakhalili, Air Quality Division Administrator, Oregon Department of Environmental Quality, Hearing on From Gridlock to Growth: Permitting Reform Under the Clean Air Act, 119th Cong. (Sept. 16, 2025).
Section 2 also amends the definition of ``modification'' to exclude projects that reduce the amount of any air pollutant, even if other more dangerous pollutants are increased as a result, or restore, maintain, or improve the reliability of operations. This is not a minor change since maintaining, improving reliability, and restoring facility operations often results in the expansion of that aging facility and leads to pollution causing construction. This is a giant loophole for old and outdated facilities to avoid controlling their pollution, not a fix for facilities trying to reduce emissions but caught in a grey area--as the majority claims.
Section 3 amends Section 169 of the CAA to redefine ``construction'' to include a modification so long as it does not lead to a ``significant emissions increase or a significant net emissions increase, in annual actual emissions at such facility.'' The vagueness of the term ``significant'' leaves enough room for large emissions to go unaccounted for and for states to have to fill the gaps for those emissions that are no longer required to be offset under the NSR program.
Section 4 amends Section 171 of the CAA to redefine ``modifications'' and ``modified'' to exempt changes that do not lead to a ``significant emissions increase or a significant net emissions increase, in annual actual emissions at such facility.'' The vagueness of the term ``significant'' leaves enough room for large emissions to go unaccounted for and for communities to have to bear the burden of additional pollution and public health harms.
At the Environment Subcommittee and Full Committee markups, the majority rejected multiple commonsense amendments to address glaring problems with this bill, including an amendment to limit implementation of this act within five miles of schools and healthcare facilities most at risk of public health harms. The majority also rejected an amendment for facilities to make all hourly emissions data available to the public so neighboring communities could know if these facilities are increasing pollution due to these new definitions. The majority also rejected an amendment to restrict older, less efficient, higher polluting coal plants from using the loopholes in the act and require that they be brought to the same standards as all other facilities.
CONCLUSION
The NSR program simply says facilities must have--and use-- control technology to reduce pollution and protect the surrounding community. This approach ensures that both the facility and community can mitigate any pollution increases before building begins, when it is most cost-effective. But this Republican bill would gut these requirements. H.R. 161 would allow massive increases in cancer causing pollution at facilities by changing how emissions are measured under the NSR program, would give sweeping exemptions to certain types of modifications at industrial facilities, which would exempt nearly every facility from having to install pollution controls.
In line with the Republicans' polluter over people agenda, H.R. 161 will drive up dangerous pollution that makes Americans sicker, so they can do the bidding of their corporate polluter friends. For the reasons stated above, we dissent from the views contained in the Committee's report.
Frank Pallone, Jr.,
Ranking Member.
